trajectories.title: Voluntary generation commitments
trajectories.summary: Developers may invest in new generation or sign long-term power contracts. These commitments remain voluntary.
trajectories.origin: Swedish business organisations favour incentives and contracts. The US pledge shows how companies can also make voluntary generation commitments under political pressure.
trajectories.example: A company signs a PPA for its own procurement goals. Another purchases from existing generation without a national requirement to add supply.
parameters: Voluntary procurement remains a behavioural assumption
trajectories.decisions: No legislation establishing a sector requirement is adopted. Companies decide their procurement commitments.
trajectories.development: 2027–2029: voluntary procurement continues. From 2030: no national requirement is introduced.

trajectories.title: Require new renewable generation
trajectories.summary: From 2030, new sites must secure new renewable generation in Sweden matching their annual electricity use, through investment or a long-term power contract.
trajectories.origin: The Swedish Green Party proposes new renewable generation matching consumption. The PPA option comes from Svenska kraftnät’s discussion. The 2030 start, first-year compliance and detailed eligibility rules are specified here so that the reform can be assessed.
trajectories.example: A site opening in 2030 must secure matching new renewable annual generation and report compliance.
parameters: Requirement starts in 2030 for new sites
100% annual demand matched by new renewable generation in Sweden
Own investment or a long-term power purchase agreement
trajectories.decisions: Government prepares legislation; Parliament establishes the requirement and Ei’s monitoring mandate.
trajectories.development: 2027–2029: prepare and adopt the requirement. From 2030: apply and maintain it for new sites.

trajectories.title: Halt new establishments
trajectories.summary: No new commercial data-centre sites may open in Sweden from 2030, including projects that offer new generation. Existing sites and their expansions remain outside the restriction.
trajectories.origin: Campaigners in Ireland call for a nationwide moratorium. Earlier pauses in electricity allocation also appear in the historical survey. Here that policy direction is specified as a Swedish stop on new openings from 2030.
trajectories.example: A proposed site cannot open even if it has secured new renewable generation.
parameters: No new commercial sites open from 2030
Existing sites and expansions continue under the common rules
Model postponed or relocated projects and any openings brought forward before 2030
trajectories.decisions: Government prepares a national restriction; Parliament establishes its legal basis, transition rules and enforcement. Authorities apply those rules in individual cases.
trajectories.development: 2027–2029: legislate and manage projects already in preparation. From 2030: prevent new openings and maintain the stop.

outside.contribution: Ireland requires new renewable generation covering 80% of annual demand, with a six-year transition. Friends of the Earth campaigns for a national moratorium and challenges the regulator’s policy, citing climate goals and household energy costs.
outside.limit: When does opposition seek tighter conditions, and when does it seek to halt expansion?
outside.heading: Generation requirements and demands for a stop
A stricter matching rule
outside.contribution: A draft decree proposes new renewable supply matched hourly for data centres above 1 MW. It illustrates a different design from annual matching.
outside.limit: How does the rule change the commitments required of developers?

outside.contribution: The White House pledge asks companies to secure new generation and protect other electricity customers from costs. The commitments are made by participating companies.
outside.heading: Commitments under political pressure
outside.limit: Could voluntary commitments develop without a national generation law?

outside.contribution: Party and agency proposals call for data centres to finance new electricity generation. Business groups favour incentives, but SKGS warns about competition for industrial connections. The Social Democrats link generation requirements to lower electricity bills.
outside.limit: Should contracts remain voluntary, and which generation would qualify under a requirement?
outside.heading: Who should finance new generation?

outside.contribution: Fingrid argues that transferring existing resources between contracts need not add capacity. Its response seeks clearer additionality rules.
outside.heading: What counts as additional?

outside.contribution: A government bill proposes moving full renewable annual matching from 2027 to 2030, citing investment conditions. The debate shows that implementation dates can change after a requirement has been introduced.
outside.limit: Can a requirement survive pressure to change its timetable?
outside.heading: Pressure to postpone a requirement

dimensions.name: Coalition alignment
dimensions.question: Who can organise support or opposition, now and later?
dimensions.description: Identify interests, organisation and influence. Examine how an actor’s position could change as the policy’s effects become visible.

T0.assessment: Business groups favour incentives and voluntary contracts. That support can fracture: SKGS already warns that data centres compete with industry for connections. If manufacturers face delays while data centres connect, they gain a reason to seek tougher conditions. Household campaigns can make higher bills an electoral cost for parties defending continuation.
T0.uncertainty: Track whether industry associations and household campaigns begin demanding conditions specifically on data-centre expansion, and whether parliamentary parties adopt those demands.

T1.assessment: The Swedish Green Party proposes a renewable-generation requirement. The Social Democrats call for data centres to contribute electricity production; together the parties hold 121 of 349 seats. EcoDataCenter supports additionality requirements. Svenska kraftnät proposes investigating a broader fossil-free requirement. Uniper wants nuclear power and lifetime extensions included. The reform has advocates, but they differ over which generation should qualify.
T1.uncertainty: A joint party proposal specifying eligible generation and a negotiating agreement with affected businesses would strengthen T1.

T2.assessment: A stop could bring together electricity consumers, industrial users facing delays and opponents of resource-intensive expansion. Irish campaigners show how that demand can be organised. In Sweden, the mapped party proposals seek production contributions, while tech organisations seek expansion. A national stop therefore needs a much larger change in political alliances than T1.
T2.uncertainty: Track whether industry associations and household campaigns begin demanding conditions specifically on data-centre expansion, and whether parliamentary parties adopt those demands.

T0-T1.judgement: T0 has the stronger starting position, but its business support is vulnerable to conflict between electricity users. T1 offers a possible agreement between expansion advocates and groups demanding that developers add supply. Its present advocates still need a wider parliamentary majority and agreement over eligible generation.
T0-T1.condition: Track whether industry associations and household campaigns begin demanding conditions specifically on data-centre expansion, and whether parliamentary parties adopt those demands.
T0-T1.takeaway: T0 starts with broader organised support. T1 needs a wider parliamentary agreement and agreement on eligible generation.

T0-T2.judgement: T0 has stronger organised support. For T2 to overtake it, electricity-cost and connection conflicts would need to produce an alliance willing to block new sites, with parties able to legislate for it.
T0-T2.condition: Track whether industry associations and household campaigns begin demanding conditions specifically on data-centre expansion, and whether parliamentary parties adopt those demands.
T0-T2.takeaway: T0 starts with stronger organised support. T2 needs a new alliance willing to halt investment.

T1-T2.judgement: T1 is easier to build an agreement around: it preserves an investment route while requiring new supply. T2 would gain ground if those commitments failed to address the grievances driving opposition.
T1-T2.condition: Track whether industry associations and household campaigns begin demanding conditions specifically on data-centre expansion, and whether parliamentary parties adopt those demands.
T1-T2.takeaway: T1 has identifiable reform advocates. A coalition for T2 would have to accept the loss of new establishments.

overview.T0: Business support can split if industry faces delays and households organise over bills.
overview.T1: Reform advocates disagree over renewables, nuclear and existing plants.
overview.T2: Needs a new alliance willing to halt investment, beyond today’s production proposals.

dimensions.guide: Who can organise support or opposition?

keep-pace.T0-T1: Industrial users have less reason to join household campaigns against expansion. T0’s business support is more likely to hold.
keep-pace.T0-T2: Fewer price and connection disputes make it harder to assemble a Swedish coalition for T2.
keep-pace.T1-T2: T1 can still unite investment and climate interests. The case for organising around T2 weakens.

pressure.T0-T1: Industrial users facing delays can join households seeking protection from rising bills. That opens a broader coalition for T1.
pressure.T0-T2: T2 can attract electricity users and delayed industrial projects, but still needs parties willing to enact a stop.
pressure.T1-T2: T1 offers a compromise between new investment and electricity users. T2 gains if that response fails to satisfy opponents.

dimensions.name: Institutional constraints
dimensions.question: Which decisions and legal constraints govern each policy?
dimensions.description: Trace the route from a political demand to a rule that authorities can apply. Distinguish formal legal constraints from political habits.

T0.assessment: Voluntary generation contracts fit the existing electricity-market framework. Continuing this arrangement requires no new sector legislation or compliance authority. Grid operators and the regulator retain their existing connection and supervision roles.
T0.uncertainty: A bill with an established legal basis, assigned supervision and a timetable would remove much of this disadvantage.

T1.assessment: In this legislative scenario, government must prepare a bill and Parliament must establish the requirement and give the Energy Markets Inspectorate (Ei) powers to monitor compliance. The bill must justify singling out new data centres and define how the requirement relates to non-discriminatory grid access.
T1.uncertainty: A bill with an established legal basis, assigned supervision and a timetable would remove much of this disadvantage.

T2.assessment: Sweden protects freedom of trade and requires impartial administration. A national moratorium would need legislation justified by an important public interest, with rules for pending projects. Politicians cannot direct the outcome of individual administrative cases covered by constitutional independence. This makes T2 a substantial legislative change; protecting selected competitors alone is not a sufficient basis.
T2.uncertainty: A government bill would establish the proposed legal basis, transition arrangements and implementing authority. For T2, the justification must address why conditions on development would be insufficient.

T0-T1.judgement: T0 can continue under existing rules. T1 requires a government bill, parliamentary approval and a monitoring mandate for Ei before implementation in 2030.
T0-T1.condition: A bill with an established legal basis, assigned supervision and a timetable would remove much of this disadvantage.
T0-T1.takeaway: T0 fits existing rules. T1 requires legislation and a monitoring mandate for Ei.

T0-T2.judgement: T0 has a clear institutional advantage. T2 must replace an open application route with a sector-wide restriction and justify the treatment of projects already underway.
T0-T2.condition: A government bill would establish the proposed legal basis, transition arrangements and implementing authority. For T2, the justification must address why conditions on development would be insufficient.
T0-T2.takeaway: T0 follows established procedures. T2 requires legislation, a public-interest justification and transition rules.

T1-T2.judgement: Both reforms need legislation. T1 creates a compliance route for new sites; T2 closes that route even for a developer willing to add generation. That broader restriction is harder to justify when less restrictive policy responses are available.
T1-T2.condition: A government bill would establish the proposed legal basis, transition arrangements and implementing authority. For T2, the justification must address why conditions on development would be insufficient.
T1-T2.takeaway: Both require legislation. T2 faces the harder task of justifying a sector-wide restriction.

overview.T0: Existing contracts and authorities are sufficient.
overview.T1: Needs legislation, a sector-specific justification and supervision.
overview.T2: Needs a justified national restriction and rules for projects already in preparation.

dimensions.guide: Which rules and decision procedures matter?

keep-pace.T0-T1: T1 still needs legislation. Timely supply gives government less urgency to overcome those procedural hurdles.
keep-pace.T0-T2: T2 still needs a legal justification and transition rules. Its political sponsors have a weaker shortage argument.
keep-pace.T1-T2: The decision procedures remain the same. T2’s sponsors have less reason to argue that conditions on development are insufficient.

pressure.T0-T1: Price and connection disputes can increase pressure for a bill. T1 still has to pass Parliament and establish supervision.
pressure.T0-T2: Urgency can put T2 on the agenda. Constitutional safeguards and rules for pending projects still govern adoption.
pressure.T1-T2: Both gain political urgency. T2 must still justify why a complete restriction is warranted.

dimensions.name: Landscape pressures
dimensions.question: How could wider change shift political priorities by 2035?
dimensions.description: Landscape pressures concern macro-level change and public opinion: the AI investment race, industrial decarbonisation, energy-price shocks and changing views of who should benefit from scarce electricity. Assess how these developments could strengthen or weaken each trajectory over time.

T0.assessment: The AI investment race and digital sovereignty favour attracting new sites. But continued demand growth without sufficient generation brings a competing priority: affordable electricity for homes and industrial electrification. Svenska kraftnät describes this price and competitiveness risk. If it persists, the political appeal of accommodating every new project weakens.
T0.uncertainty: Follow changes in electricity affordability, industrial project delays, energy security and public attitudes to data-centre growth. New generation that keeps pace with demand would weaken the case for tighter restrictions.

T1.assessment: A generation requirement can accommodate AI investment while responding to industrial decarbonisation and concern over bills. Its political appeal grows if the wider debate shifts from attracting investment towards who supplies the electricity and who benefits. The Swedish party proposals already combine these priorities.
T1.uncertainty: Follow changes in electricity affordability, industrial project delays, energy security and public attitudes to data-centre growth. New generation that keeps pace with demand would weaken the case for tighter restrictions.

T2.assessment: A prolonged energy crisis, delayed industrial investment and a public view that expansion serves foreign firms at households’ expense could make a stop politically attractive. Irish campaigners express this resource-priority argument. In Sweden it would compete with the ambitions for AI capacity and digital sovereignty, which favour maintaining a route for new investment.
T2.uncertainty: Follow changes in electricity affordability, industrial project delays, energy security and public attitudes to data-centre growth. New generation that keeps pace with demand would weaken the case for tighter restrictions.

T0-T1.judgement: T0 benefits most while attracting AI investment is the dominant priority. T1 gains if energy affordability and industrial electrification become more pressing. The comparison follows how demand, supply and public debate develop together.
T0-T1.condition: Follow changes in electricity affordability, industrial project delays, energy security and public attitudes to data-centre growth. New generation that keeps pace with demand would weaken the case for tighter restrictions.
T0-T1.takeaway: T0 fits the drive to attract AI investment. T1 also addresses concern over electricity prices and industrial electrification.

T0-T2.judgement: T0 fits the present digital-investment agenda more closely. T2 becomes a serious competitor if persistent shortages and price pressure make limiting new demand a widely accepted public priority.
T0-T2.condition: Follow changes in electricity affordability, industrial project delays, energy security and public attitudes to data-centre growth. New generation that keeps pace with demand would weaken the case for tighter restrictions.
T0-T2.takeaway: T0 fits current digital-investment ambitions. T2 gains relevance when limiting electricity demand becomes a political priority.

T1-T2.judgement: T1 can respond to competing priorities without stopping investment. T2 gains relative to it if the public problem becomes total resource use or connection displacement, which an annual generation requirement does not settle.
T1-T2.condition: Follow changes in electricity affordability, industrial project delays, energy security and public attitudes to data-centre growth. New generation that keeps pace with demand would weaken the case for tighter restrictions.
T1-T2.takeaway: T1 combines continued investment with new generation. T2 gains if opposition concerns the scale of expansion itself.

overview.T0: AI competition favours expansion; persistent price pressure can reverse that advantage.
overview.T1: Can reconcile digital investment with growing demands for affordable electricity.
overview.T2: Becomes more attractive if an energy crisis changes public priorities against expansion.

dimensions.framework_reference: Fornborg (2026), §4.3 and Table 1; Geels (2002), reference 31 in the article.
dimensions.guide: How could wider trends change political priorities?

keep-pace.T0-T1: AI investment and electrification can advance together. The price-driven case for T1 weakens, while climate priorities can sustain support.
keep-pace.T0-T2: Continued investment sits more comfortably with affordable electricity. T0 retains the stronger position.
keep-pace.T1-T2: Climate and investment priorities can support T1. T2’s resource-priority argument becomes less pressing.

pressure.T0-T1: Affordability and industrial competitiveness challenge the AI-investment agenda. T1 becomes more attractive as a way to reconcile them.
pressure.T0-T2: Persistent shortages make limiting new demand more politically attractive. That reduces T0’s advantage over T2.
pressure.T1-T2: T1 gains from demand for new supply. T2 gains further if debate centres on land, connections and the total scale of expansion.

dimensions.name: Adjustment burden
dimensions.question: Who loses, how can they adjust, and what influence do they have?
dimensions.description: Assess losses under continuation as well as reform. Include the capacity to absorb costs, secure compensation or turn those costs into political opposition.

T0.assessment: If new demand outpaces supply, households and industrial users face higher electricity bills. Firms can also lose years of investment returns while waiting for network capacity. Households can cut other spending or electricity use; firms can hedge, delay or relocate investment. SKGS represents industrial users in energy policy. Bensinupproret illustrates how household fuel costs can lead to organised demands for lower taxes.
T0.uncertainty: Reassess when bills, delayed projects or cancelled investments become politically salient. For T1, check whether generation delivery dates leave developers a workable route to comply.

T1.assessment: New data-centre developers must finance generation or commit to long-term payments under a PPA. The contract option avoids having to build and operate a power plant themselves. However, T1 requires the new plant to be ready when the data centre opens: a delayed generation project can therefore delay the data centre. Developers can respond by seeking exemptions, postponement or a different location. SweDCI’s demands for timetable guarantees show why this matters politically.
T1.uncertainty: A phase-in or protection against generation-project delays would reduce developers’ resistance. Grid reinforcement charges require a separate decision: neither trajectory changes who pays them.

T2.assessment: Developers lose the option to open new sites; projects already in preparation face write-downs or relocation. Host municipalities lose expected investment and jobs. Firms with existing sites retain an expansion route under this example’s definition. Those uneven losses create pressure for exemptions, an earlier end date or compensation. Consumers avoid this cohort’s added demand, but that benefit must be weighed against the concentrated opposition.
T2.uncertainty: Reassess when bills, delayed projects or cancelled investments become politically salient. For T1, check whether generation delivery dates leave developers a workable route to comply.

T0-T1.judgement: T0 leaves more of the risk from inadequate new supply with other electricity users. T1 assigns developers a financing obligation and gives them a contractual way to comply. It is easier to defend as a response to price pressure, but first-year compliance can delay openings and organise industry resistance around the timetable.
T0-T1.condition: Reassess when bills, delayed projects or cancelled investments become politically salient. For T1, check whether generation delivery dates leave developers a workable route to comply.
T0-T1.takeaway: T0 exposes other users to the costs of inadequate supply. T1 places generation costs and delivery risks on developers.

T0-T2.judgement: T2 removes this cohort’s new electricity demand and the associated pressure on other users. Its losses are more concentrated and politically organised than under T0: developers cannot comply their way into opening. Sustaining the stop therefore requires a coalition prepared to defend those losses.
T0-T2.condition: Reassess when bills, delayed projects or cancelled investments become politically salient. For T1, check whether generation delivery dates leave developers a workable route to comply.
T0-T2.takeaway: T2 reduces pressure from new demand, while concentrating losses on developers and prospective host communities.

T1-T2.judgement: T1 gives developers an adjustment route through investment or a power contract; T2 removes the investment opportunity altogether. That makes T1 easier to sustain against business and municipal opposition, provided generation can be delivered on the required timetable.
T1-T2.condition: Reassess when bills, delayed projects or cancelled investments become politically salient. For T1, check whether generation delivery dates leave developers a workable route to comply.
T1-T2.takeaway: T1 offers developers a contractual route to open. T2 closes that route, increasing their incentive to oppose it.

overview.T0: Higher bills and delayed industrial projects can create organised opposition.
overview.T1: Developers must finance new plants or sign long-term power contracts.
overview.T2: Blocked projects concentrate losses on developers and host municipalities.

dimensions.guide: Who loses, and how can they adjust?

keep-pace.T0-T1: Other users face less pressure from new demand. T1’s financing and delivery obligations remain visible to developers.
keep-pace.T0-T2: The relief T2 offers electricity users is smaller. Developers and host communities still lose planned projects.
keep-pace.T1-T2: T1 retains a route for investment through generation contracts. T2 still imposes concentrated project losses.

pressure.T0-T1: Higher bills and investment delays make T0’s losses more visible. T1 shifts generation financing to developers, who may resist its timetable.
pressure.T0-T2: More electricity users have reasons to support restrictions. Developers and host communities have reasons to organise against T2.
pressure.T1-T2: T1 can address supply costs while allowing projects to proceed. T2 gains support if those conditions fail to protect other users.

dimensions.name: Policy momentum
dimensions.question: How do previous decisions and new effects change the policy’s support?
dimensions.description: Previous policies establish routines, investments and expectations. Their effects can also create new interests that defend the policy or seek to reverse it.

T0.assessment: Contracting and established connection procedures make continuation easier initially. But momentum can turn: Sweden withdrew the data-centre electricity-tax concession in 2023. If further expansion raises bills or obstructs industrial investment, defending the existing policy becomes more costly and earlier supporters may seek reform.
T0.uncertainty: Track policy feedback: whether voluntary contracts deliver new supply, whether losses shift organised support, and whether adopted requirements or a stop survive pressure for postponement and exemptions.

T1.assessment: The question has moved into party programmes and Svenska kraftnät’s recommendations. Ireland has adopted an additional-renewable-electricity requirement, providing a practical precedent. Sweden would still need to establish its own compliance system. Germany’s proposal to postpone renewable matching shows how investment concerns can reopen a requirement’s timetable after adoption.
T1.uncertainty: A Swedish implementation programme and completed projects meeting the requirement would strengthen expectations that it will continue.

T2.assessment: A national stop departs sharply from investment promotion and case-by-case administration. Firms and municipalities already preparing projects have reasons to resist it. If adopted, the stop could build support among users who benefit from reduced demand, while developers press for exceptions or reopening. Holding it until 2035 is a separate political task from passing it.
T2.uncertainty: Track policy feedback: whether voluntary contracts deliver new supply, whether losses shift organised support, and whether adopted requirements or a stop survive pressure for postponement and exemptions.

T0-T1.judgement: T0 has the advantage of existing practice. T1 is already on the policy agenda and could gain further support as the costs of continuation become visible. After adoption, new generation contracts would give investors an interest in stable rules, while developers could still press to postpone compliance.
T0-T1.condition: Track policy feedback: whether voluntary contracts deliver new supply, whether losses shift organised support, and whether adopted requirements or a stop survive pressure for postponement and exemptions.
T0-T1.takeaway: T0 benefits from established practice. T1 builds on reform proposals and precedents for generation requirements.

T0-T2.judgement: T0 has a strong initial advantage. Repeated failures to manage prices and connections could undermine it, but introducing and maintaining a national stop would require a much larger departure from Swedish practice.
T0-T2.condition: Track policy feedback: whether voluntary contracts deliver new supply, whether losses shift organised support, and whether adopted requirements or a stop survive pressure for postponement and exemptions.
T0-T2.takeaway: T0 extends existing practice. T2 disrupts investment plans and creates pressure for exemptions.

T1-T2.judgement: T1 extends an existing reform agenda and familiar contracting arrangements. T2 is a sharper break, with stronger incentives for affected firms to seek exemptions or repeal. This favours T1 both at adoption and during implementation.
T1-T2.condition: Track policy feedback: whether voluntary contracts deliver new supply, whether losses shift organised support, and whether adopted requirements or a stop survive pressure for postponement and exemptions.
T1-T2.takeaway: T1 develops existing proposals. T2 is a larger break with investment promotion and individual project decisions.

overview.T0: Established routines favour continuation, but mounting losses can erode that support.
overview.T1: Party proposals and agency work advance reform; firms can press for postponement.
overview.T2: Breaks with investment promotion; existing projects create pressure for exceptions.

dimensions.guide: What do earlier policies and investments set in motion?

keep-pace.T0-T1: Voluntary contracts that deliver supply reinforce T0. T1 remains on the agenda through its existing advocates.
keep-pace.T0-T2: Successful expansion strengthens the expectations and investments behind T0. A stop becomes harder to maintain.
keep-pace.T1-T2: If T1 is adopted, generation contracts can create supporters of stable rules. A stop continues to face pressure to reopen.

pressure.T0-T1: Costs of continuation can turn former supporters towards T1. Once adopted, generation investments can help sustain the requirement.
pressure.T0-T2: Repeated failures to address costs can weaken support for T0. T2 would then face continued lobbying for exceptions and reopening.
pressure.T1-T2: T1 can gain momentum through legislation and new contracts. T2 becomes more plausible if implementation repeatedly disappoints.

actors.name: Swedish Parliament
actors.position_overall: The Green Party and Social Democrats together hold 121 of 349 seats. A broader parliamentary agreement is needed for their production proposals.
actors.policy_question: T1 and T2 require parliamentary approval.

actors.name: Svenska kraftnät
actors.capacity: Transmission-system operator; advises government and develops connection policy.
actors.position_overall: Proposes investigating generation requirements for major new electricity demand, considering fossil-free supply, timing and location.
actors.policy_question: Supports investigation of reform; its design is broader than annual renewable matching.

actors.name: Energy Markets Inspectorate (Ei)
actors.capacity: Regulates electricity networks and reviews connection conditions.
actors.position_overall: Stresses non-discriminatory grid access and the risk that preferential AI arrangements displace other electricity users.
actors.policy_question: T1 assigns a new compliance role that legislation must establish.

actors.name: EcoDataCenter
actors.capacity: Invests in and operates data centres; participates in energy-policy debate.
actors.position_overall: Calls for incentives and additionality requirements, while criticising connection conditions that conflict with its operating model.
actors.policy_question: Additionality requirements would make developers increase electricity supply.

actors.name: Swedish Data Center Industry (SweDCI)
actors.capacity: Industry association; represents data-centre companies in policy discussions.
actors.position_overall: Seeks incentives, timetable guarantees and coordination. Describes long-term power purchase agreements as important for generation and location.
actors.policy_question: Its proposals favour negotiated investment arrangements.

actors.name: SKGS · energy-intensive industries
actors.capacity: Represents forest, chemical, mining and steel industries.
actors.position_overall: Questions compulsory long-term power contracts, while warning that rapid data-centre growth competes with industry for power and grid connections.
actors.policy_question: Its defence of voluntary contracting may weaken if member firms’ own investments are displaced. This is a possible change in position over the scenario period.

actors.name: Swedish Green Party
actors.capacity: Parliamentary party; 22 seats after the 2026 election.
actors.position_overall: Proposes requiring data centres to invest in new renewable electricity production corresponding to their consumption.
actors.policy_question: The clearest party advocate for the renewable scope used in T1.

actors.name: Svenskt Näringsliv · business confederation
actors.capacity: Coordinates business interests and seeks changes to national policy.
actors.position_overall: Proposes incentives for new-generation contracts, faster permits and connection charges that protect other customers from cost transfers.
actors.policy_question: Supports an incentive-led route; the proposed tariff changes are separate from the generation requirement.

actors.name: TechSverige
actors.capacity: Tech-industry association; represents firms in digital and industrial policy.
actors.position_overall: Wants predictable investment conditions, faster electricity infrastructure and lower electricity tax. It accepts that tax relief may come with locally adapted sustainability conditions.
actors.policy_question: Supports sustainability conditions adapted to each location.

actors.name: Swedish Social Democratic Party
actors.capacity: Parliamentary party; 99 seats after the 2026 election.
actors.position_overall: Its August 2026 election pledge calls for data centres to contribute electricity production as part of reducing electricity bills.
actors.policy_question: Advocates production contributions within a broader fossil-free energy programme.

actors.name: Uniper
actors.capacity: Electricity producer and investor; can finance generation and negotiate supply contracts.
actors.position_overall: Proposes incentives for data-centre investment in generation. If matching requirements are imposed, it wants nuclear power and lifetime extensions to count.
actors.policy_question: A potential reform partner with a concrete objection to T1’s eligible-generation rules.

scope.question: Which rules for new Swedish data centres could be adopted and sustained as electricity demand grows?
scope.policy: A national requirement on developers to secure additional generation
scope.cohort: The same prospective projects are assessed in all three alternatives: new commercial data-centre sites in Sweden that would open from 2030. Existing sites and their expansions fall outside this example.
scope.shared: Electricity demand and the rules already in place form the common starting point. T0 keeps generation commitments voluntary; T1 makes new generation a condition of opening; T2 prevents new sites from opening from 2030. Grid tariffs and queue priorities are not changed by these alternatives.
scope.timing: Assess decisions in 2027–2030 and whether the resulting policy can be sustained to 2035. The dates are scenario choices. Political support can change within this period.
scope.definition: From the first full operating year, new renewable generation in Sweden must match 100% of each covered data centre’s annual electricity demand. Developers invest directly or sign a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA). The generating plant must enter service after the investment or contract commitment and by the data centre’s opening. The reform includes annual compliance reporting to the Energy Markets Inspectorate (Ei), with powers granted by the new legislation. Grid charges and connection priority remain as in T0.

overall.title: Continuation is easier initially; a generation requirement can gain support
overall.judgement: For adoption by 2030, T0 has the strongest starting position: established procedures and organised support for voluntary contracts. T1 has a viable route through existing reform proposals, but needs a wider parliamentary agreement, agreement over eligible generation and a workable compliance timetable. T2 faces the greatest obstacles: a new coalition, a justified sector-wide restriction and resistance from planned investments.
overall.reason: That ordering need not last to 2035. If supply and networks lag behind demand, higher bills and delayed industrial projects can unite voters and industry behind stricter conditions. T1 is better placed than a complete stop to combine continued investment with new supply. T2 becomes more plausible if those responses repeatedly fail or opposition comes to concern the scale of expansion itself.
overall.model: Use T0 as the reference for initial policy continuation, test T1 as the principal reform, and include T2 as a less feasible but consequential alternative. Assess both a period in which supply keeps pace and one in which price and connection pressures grow. Reassess political support as those conditions change.
overall.revisit: Revisit the judgement when industrial users change their demands, household campaigns target data-centre growth, parties change position, or legislation advances.

model_note: For T0 and T1, model voluntary procurement as well as the statutory generation requirement in T1. For T2, set new openings in the defined cohort to zero from 2030 and allow for postponed or relocated projects. Existing sites and expansions remain in every case. Use resulting prices, investment delays and distributional effects to reconsider political support over time.
derivation: The survey points to voluntary commitments, generation requirements and restrictions on new sites. These three alternatives apply those policy directions to new commercial data centres in Sweden from 2030.

actor_conflicts.title: Incentives or a legal requirement?
actor_conflicts.text: Svenskt Näringsliv and SweDCI propose incentives for generation contracts. SKGS questions compulsory long-term contracts in the connection process, but also warns that data centres may displace industrial projects. The business coalition can split as access to electricity becomes more contested.

actor_conflicts.title: Support for reform, different proposals
actor_conflicts.text: The Swedish Green Party calls for new renewable generation. The Social Democrats want data centres to contribute electricity production, and EcoDataCenter supports additionality requirements. Svenska kraftnät proposes investigating fossil-free generation. Uniper wants nuclear power and lifetime extensions included.

actor_conflicts.title: Who gets electricity, and who pays?
actor_conflicts.text: SKGS warns that data centres compete with industrial projects for power and grid connections. The Social Democrats link production commitments by data centres to lower household electricity bills. Rising costs and delayed investments can increase pressure for conditions on expansion.

method_dynamics.title: Assess how political conditions can change
method_dynamics.intro: Landscape pressures are changes in the wider political, economic and cultural setting: energy crises, industrial change, the AI investment race and shifts in public opinion. Look for developments that could change what governments prioritise during the scenario period.
method_dynamics.link: Then trace who gains or loses, how affected groups could organise, and which policy changes they could secure. Actor roles can change: a group that accepts today’s policy may campaign against it when its costs grow.

political_development.title: Follow a possible conflict through to 2035
political_development.intro: Current evidence supplies the starting conditions. The following sequence is a prospective assessment of how they could alter policy support.

stages.title: Electricity demand grows faster than supply
stages.text: AI investment and industrial electrification expand at the same time. Svenska kraftnät expects rising prices and weaker industrial competitiveness if new generation persistently falls behind demand.

stages.title: Bills rise and industrial projects wait
stages.text: Households have less money left after electricity bills. Industrial firms face higher operating costs and delayed investments where network capacity is scarce. SKGS already warns of competition with data centres for power and connections.

stages.title: Affected groups press for different rules
stages.text: Firms can organise through industry associations; households can campaign, petition and vote. Bensinupproret’s 2019 fuel-tax protests illustrate that route to political pressure. If households attribute higher electricity bills to data-centre growth, demands for generation requirements or an establishment stop could gain support.

political_development.consequence: The inside view then asks whether these demands can pass through Sweden’s decision procedures, and whether previous policy and investments help or obstruct them. A requirement could attract firms and voters who want new generation but oppose a complete stop. A stop becomes more plausible if other responses repeatedly fail.
political_development.alternative: If new generation and grid investment keep pace, the basis for that alliance weakens. Electricity prices, industrial connection delays, organised demands and parties’ responses are therefore signs to track as the scenario develops.

historical_mobilisation.title: Bensinupproret · Sweden, 2019
historical_mobilisation.text: Bensinupproret organised motorists through social media and demonstrations, demanding lower fuel taxes. Participants stressed the cost of commuting and their dependence on cars outside cities. A parliamentary motion cited the movement in proposing a halt to further fuel-tax increases; Parliament rejected it.
historical_mobilisation.method_question: When could household energy costs turn into organised demands to change policy?

history_previews.crypto: Power allocation changed when regional benefits came under scrutiny.
history_previews.wind: Compensation and local ownership became part of wind policy.
history_previews.bensin: Household fuel costs became organised demands for lower taxes.

actor_previews.title: Business interests can diverge
actor_previews.text: Data-centre investment and industrial electrification compete for connections. SKGS already raises this conflict.

actor_previews.title: Reform has advocates
actor_previews.text: Parties and energy companies propose generation requirements, with disagreement over which plants should qualify.

actor_previews.title: Costs can change political support
actor_previews.text: Higher household bills and delayed industrial projects can create pressure for stricter conditions on expansion.

developments.label: Supply and grids keep pace
developments.description: New generation and network capacity accommodate growing demand through 2035. Price and connection pressures ease.

chain.label: Wider change
chain.text: AI investment and industrial electrification proceed with fewer conflicts over electricity.

chain.label: Costs and adjustment
chain.text: Households and industry face less pressure from bills and delayed connections.

chain.label: Political response
chain.text: The alliance for stricter conditions has less reason to form. Climate and investment interests remain.

results.T0: Timely supply and connections strengthen the case for keeping commitments voluntary.
results.T1: Existing reform advocates remain, but the price-driven case for a requirement weakens.
results.T2: Reduced pressure on other users makes a national stop harder to justify politically.

developments.model: Use T0 as the reference for policy continuation and test T1 as a reform alternative. T2 remains a more distant possibility.

developments.label: Prices and connection queues rise
developments.description: Demand outpaces new generation and network capacity through 2035. Electricity bills rise and industrial projects wait.

chain.label: Wider change
chain.text: Affordable electricity and industrial competitiveness compete with the drive to attract AI investment.

chain.label: Costs and adjustment
chain.text: Households cut other spending. Industrial firms delay, reduce or relocate investment.

chain.label: Political response
chain.text: Industry associations and household campaigns can seek stronger conditions on new data centres.

developments.result_title: A generation requirement can gain broader support

results.T0: Rising costs and industrial delays can divide the coalition behind voluntary commitments.
results.T1: New-generation requirements offer a possible agreement between investment advocates and electricity users.
results.T2: A stop becomes more plausible if other responses fail or opposition targets the scale of expansion itself.

developments.model: Test T1 as the principal reform and T2 as a consequential alternative. Reconsider continued support for T0 as losses and organised opposition grow.
